title: Choosing the Correct Built-In Module
learning_outcomes: Explain choosing the correct built-in module and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply choosing the correct built-in module in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Choosing the Correct Built-In Module** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect math-related tasks with color-related tasks, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: Dart Sass groups built-ins into namespaced modules such as `sass:math`, `sass:color`, `sass:list`, `sass:map`, `sass:string`, `sass:meta`, and `sass:selector`. Load the module you need and read its argument and return-value contract.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Keep compiler-time calculations separate from CSS functions that should run in the browser. Test missing keys, invalid indices, unit compatibility, and color-space assumptions instead of hiding errors behind a fallback.

items.title: Math-related tasks
items.text: For math-related tasks, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Color-related tasks
items.text: Choose a namespaced `sass:color` operation that matches the task, and document the color space. For runtime theme changes, consider CSS custom properties instead of compiling a new color.

items.title: List and map operations
items.text: Identify the collection, the per-item rule, and the stopping condition. Validate collection shape and inspect the count and naming of generated rules.

items.title: String manipulation
items.text: For string manipulation, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Metadata and dynamic loading
items.text: For metadata and dynamic loading, identify the relevant source rule, predict the intended result, and check the emitted CSS against that expectation.

items.title: Selector manipulation
items.text: Predict the expanded selector before compiling. Keep nesting shallow and verify that the emitted selector does not match more elements than intended.

items.title: Separating Sass operations from browser-native CSS functions
items.text: A Sass function should return a value that can be used in an expression. Keep side effects out of its purpose and report missing or invalid input clearly.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates choosing the correct built-in module. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates choosing the correct built-in module. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates choosing the correct built-in module. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
